questions.q: State de Broglie's wavelength formula and identify each variable with its SI unit.
questions.a: λ = h/(mv) where λ = wavelength (m), h = Planck's constant (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s), m = mass of particle (kg), v = velocity (m/s). A wrong answer (e.g., λ = h/mv² or missing h) reveals the student is memorising without understanding the momentum analogy from photon physics.

questions.q: Why does a baseball (mass 0.15 kg, speed 40 m/s) not exhibit observable diffraction while an electron (mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, speed 10⁶ m/s) does? Calculate both wavelengths to justify.
questions.a: Baseball: λ = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(0.15×40) ≈ 1.1×10⁻³⁴ m. Electron: λ = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(9.11×10⁻³¹×10⁶) ≈ 7.3×10⁻¹⁰ m. The baseball's wavelength is ~10²⁴ times smaller than atomic spacing, making diffraction impossible. A student who only compares masses without calculating misses the combined mass-velocity effect.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength. (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
questions.a: Step 1: Kinetic energy gained = eV = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ × 100 = 1.602×10⁻¹⁷ J. Step 2: KE = ½mv² → v = √(2KE/m) = √(2×1.602×10⁻¹⁷/9.11×10⁻³¹) ≈ 5.93×10⁶ m/s. Step 3: λ = h/(mv) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(9.11×10⁻³¹×5.93×10⁶) ≈ 1.23×10⁻¹⁰ m = 1.23 Å. A student using λ = h/√(2meV) directly shows deeper understanding; one forgetting to convert eV to joules reveals unit confusion.

questions.q: Derive Bohr's angular momentum quantisation condition (mvr = nh/2π) from de Broglie's standing wave requirement for an electron in a circular orbit.
questions.a: For a standing wave, circumference = nλ → 2πr = n(h/mv) → mvr = nh/2π. This shows Bohr's postulate isn't arbitrary but a consequence of wave nature. A student writing 2πr = nλ but failing to substitute λ = h/mv misses the connection between wave and particle pictures.

questions.q: Evaluate: "de Broglie's hypothesis applies only to electrons." Justify your answer with two examples of other particles showing wave behaviour.
questions.a: False. The hypothesis applies to ALL matter. Examples: (1) Neutron diffraction (λ ≈ 1–10 Å) used for crystal structure determination. (2) Fullerenes (C₆₀ molecules, mass ~720 u) showed interference fringes in 1999 Vienna experiment. A student saying "only electrons" hasn't grasped the universal nature of the hypothesis.

questions.q: Design a thought experiment to determine whether a macroscopic object (e.g., a car of mass 1000 kg moving at 30 m/s) could ever show measurable wave properties. What fundamental limitation would you encounter?
questions.a: λ = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(1000×30) ≈ 2.2×10⁻³⁸ m. To observe diffraction, slit width ~λ is needed, but this is 10²³ times smaller than Planck length (1.6×10⁻³⁵ m), where spacetime itself loses meaning. Even theoretically, quantum gravity effects dominate. A good answer recognises the Planck scale barrier; a poor answer just says "too small" without quantitative comparison.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: de Broglie's hypothesis states that all matter exhibits wave-particle duality: any particle with momentum *p* has an associated wavelength λ = *h*/*p* (where *h* is Planck's constant), meaning electrons and other ______ particles behave as both particles and waves.
Fill in the blank: Observe how an ______ microscope in a biology lab can magnify viruses 15 million times while a light microscope maxes at ~2000×.

Fill in the blank: Finally, show how Bohr's arbitrary angular momentum rule (mvr = nh/______π) emerges naturally when we require the electron wave to form a standing wave around the nucleus (circumference = nλ).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can derive de Broglie's relation from photon momentum analogy, calculate wavelengths for microscopic and macroscopic objects, explain why macroscopic objects don't show observable wave properties, and connect the hypothesis to Bohr's angular momentum quantisation condition (2πr = nλ).
